lesson_title: Can You Cycle Up That Hill?
hook_text: Give me two heights and a ruler, and I will tell you if you can cycle up a hill you have never seen.
clip_script: Two points on a map. A spot height at 1 420 metres. A trig station at 1 680 metres. Can you cycle between them? First, look at the brown contour lines. Each one joins places at the same height, 20 metres apart. Packed close together? Steep. Far apart? Gentle. Now put a number on it. Gradient equals up over along. Up: 1 680 minus 1 420, that is 260 metres. Along: measure on the map, 4 centimetres. On a 1 to 50 000 map that is 2 000 metres. Both in metres, always. 260 over 2 000. Divide by 260 and you get 1 to 7,7. For every metre you climb, you ride 7,7 metres forward. Low gear, but you will make it. 1 to 3? Get off and walk. 1 to 50? You will barely notice it. The smaller the second number, the steeper the hill.
visual_style: A map with two marked points; brown contours pulse closer together on one side; a ruler measures 4 cm; numbers stack into VI over HE; a cyclist icon tilts up a slope labelled 1:7,7, then a staircase for 1:3 and a flat road for 1:50.
pacing: Quick hook, steady calculation, punchy comparison at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for contour rules, convex and concave slopes and full gradient working.
